To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) falls research evidence is presented in a variety of formats, including narrative reviews, systematic reviews, and clinical guidelines; (2) falls research evidence can be presented in a variety formats, including narrative, tabular, and graphical; (3) falls research evidence should be presented in the same format as other research evidence; (4) falls research evidence that is presented in the same formats as other research evidence can be used by policy makers and clinicians to make decisions about falls interventions; and
the evidence base for fall prevention interventions is growing, and that a number of interventions have been shown to be effective in reducing falls.

(1) the evidence base for fall risk assessment and prevention in the elderly is growing, (2) the quality and quantity of the evidence varies, and (3) there is a paucity of evidence on the effectiveness of fall prevention interventions in community-dwelling elderly people.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how to best communicate falls research evidence to policy-makers, with the aim of influencing policy and practice.
the development and evaluation of a novel approach to the design and delivery of an evidence-based falls prevention program for older adults.
determining the policy-relevant formats that can be used to present falls research evidence.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evidence does not support the effectiveness of any particular intervention to prevent falls in the older population.
the evidence does not support the use of any of the four commonly used fall prevention exercise programs in older people living in the community.
the evidence supports the effectiveness of the interventions in reducing falls in the elderly.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the research evidence is not always presented in formats that are accessible to the policy makers who are responsible for making decisions about falls prevention in Australia.
we have identified a number of key areas for future research in this field.

the presentation of falls prevention research is not consistent across the literature, with some articles presenting results in a format which makes them easier to understand for policy makers and other non-researchers.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the evidence base on fall risk factors and interventions is growing rapidly.
the evidence for the effectiveness of falls prevention programmes is strong.
there is no single best format for the presentation of evidence.
